nameStory: The Lined Water Jelly gets its name from the distinctive linear patterns visible along its bell-shaped body. These "lines" are actually radial canals that transport nutrients throughout the jellyfish, creating a beautiful geometric design that makes this species instantly recognizable underwater.
description: The Lined Water Jelly is a small, translucent marine jellyfish that drifts through New England's coastal waters. This delicate creature has a bell-shaped body with clearly visible radial lines running from the center to the edge, giving it a spoke-like appearance. Like other hydrozoans, it's actually a colony of tiny animals working together, though it looks and acts like a single jellyfish. These jellies are relatively small and almost crystal-clear, making them challenging to spot in the water.

idTips.label: Radial Lines
idTips.description: Look for distinct linear canals radiating outward from the center of the bell like spokes on a wheel - these lines are the jelly's defining feature

idTips.label: Bell Shape
idTips.description: The body forms a classic dome or bell shape that pulses rhythmically as it swims through the water

idTips.label: Transparency
idTips.description: The entire body is nearly transparent with a glass-like quality that makes it almost invisible except for the visible internal structures

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: These are relatively small jellies that won't fill your palm, much smaller than the large moon jellies you might see washed up on beaches

idTips.label: Swimming Motion
idTips.description: Moves with gentle, rhythmic pulsing contractions of its bell, creating a graceful up-and-down motion through the water column

habitat: Look for Lined Water Jellies in the open waters off New England's Atlantic coast, particularly in deeper offshore areas. They're pelagic creatures, meaning they live in the water column rather than near the bottom or shore. You're most likely to encounter them while boat watching, snorkeling in deeper water, or occasionally washed into harbors and bays during certain tide and wind conditions.

seasonality.spring: Early sightings may occur as waters begin to warm, though they're still relatively uncommon during this season.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for observations when warmer waters and calmer seas make boat-based viewing most productive. This is when you're most likely to spot them during offshore excursions.
seasonality.fall: Still present in warming waters, though sightings may become less frequent as temperatures begin to drop.
seasonality.winter: Rarely observed during cold winter months when most people aren't venturing into offshore waters for marine life viewing.

funFact: Scientists still don't know what the baby polyp stage of this jellyfish looks like - it's one of the ocean's unsolved mysteries, despite the adult form being found along coastlines from New England to Africa!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small, transparent jellies in New England waters. The key difference is those distinctive radial lines - if you can see spoke-like canals radiating from center to edge, you've found a Lined Water Jelly. Remember: "Lines equal Lined Water Jelly."
contextualKnowledge: As a hydrozoan, this isn't technically a "true" jellyfish like the moon jellies people find on beaches, but rather a colonial organism more closely related to Portuguese man-of-wars. However, it looks and behaves so much like a jellyfish that the distinction is mainly important to marine biologists.
compareHints: Since this is the only Rhacostoma species in our waters, compare it to other small aequoreids in the many-ribbed jelly family. The Lined Water Jelly's diagnostic radial lines are much more pronounced and clearly defined than the subtle markings on most other transparent jellies. While other family members may have faint internal structures, none display the bold, spoke-like pattern that makes this species unmistakable.
